messages.content: Where will this system run? The options are company servers, a cloud account, a managed platform, or nothing decided yet. It matters because the hosting choice shapes the architecture, the running cost and the compliance defaults we set later. If you are not sure, we can leave it open for now.

Thanks, that's clear. The participant has answered the hosting question, so I'm recording it and moving on. Next, I'd like to confirm the problem itself: is the double entry of nurse notes the main pain point, or are there related frictions, such as delays or transcription errors? Pick the closest option.

The main pain point is definitely the double entry of nurse notes—it's the primary source of frustration and error. Nurses report spending an average of 12 minutes per shift manually re-entering the same clinical observations into both the bedside monitoring system and the electronic health record (EHR), leading to documented delays in documentation and transcription errors in 7% of cases, as validated by a recent audit.

That's a useful detail: 12 minutes per shift and a 7% error rate give us concrete targets to measure against later. Next, which existing systems must this work with? Name the bedside monitoring system, the EHR, the spreadsheet, or anything else. It matters because every system we connect to adds integration work and data rules. Default if unsure: none.

The system must integrate with the bedside monitoring system (Philips IntelliVue X4), the EHR (Epic System version 2023.01, using FHIR R4 APIs), and the current spreadsheet used for shift handovers (a secure SharePoint document under Azure AD access control). The spreadsheet is still in use for legacy handover workflows, so we must support read/write operations via a scheduled sync every 15 minutes to avoid data loss.

The participant has now answered this, so I'm recording it and not asking again. Systems in scope: Philips IntelliVue X4 monitoring, Epic EHR (FHIR R4), and the SharePoint handover spreadsheet with a 15-minute sync. Next, we'll cover the users who would work in this system.

The primary users are ward nurses, specifically those on adult medical and surgical units—approximately 140 nurses across the hospital group. They’ll use the system via a web app accessible through the hospital’s Azure AD single sign-on, with role-based access control: only nurses assigned to a specific ward can enter notes for that ward.
Thanks for the detail on the nurses. Before we go further into users, one question: who will build this? Default if unsure: a coding agent. It shapes how the specification and plan are phrased.

Noted: an in-house team will build it. Next, let's pin down the users. Which roles besides ward nurses will use the system, such as charge nurses, ward managers or administrators? Default if unsure: ward nurses only.

Charge nurses and ward managers will also use the system, but with read-only access to all notes entered on their assigned wards. They’ll use it to monitor documentation completeness and identify delays during shift handovers. Administrators will have full access to audit logs and system settings, but only for troubleshooting and compliance reporting.

Thanks for the role details: charge nurses and ward managers get read-only access on their wards, and administrators get audit and settings access for troubleshooting and compliance.

What does the in-house team know best? Examples are a language, framework, or cloud platform. A stack the team already knows usually beats a marginally better one they must learn, so this shapes the technical choices we make next. Default if unsure: unknown.

The in-house team is proficient in C#, .NET 8, Azure Functions, and Azure SQL Database, with extensive experience in integrating FHIR APIs into Epic via Azure AD-protected OAuth 2.0 flows. They also have strong familiarity with Azure Application Gateway for secure API routing and Azure Monitor for logging and alerting. We’ll align the architecture with these strengths to reduce ramp-up time and ensure maintainability.

The team's skills are now clear: C#, .NET 8, Azure Functions, Azure SQL Database, FHIR integration with Epic, Azure AD OAuth, Application Gateway and Azure Monitor. I'm recording this and won't ask again.

Next, the technical stack: which backend framework should we use? Default: ASP.NET Core on .NET 8, since it matches the team's skills.

I confirm: the backend will use ASP.NET Core on .NET 8, as it aligns with the team’s expertise and seamlessly integrates with Azure Functions for event-driven processing, especially for the 15-minute SharePoint sync. The FHIR R4 endpoints will be built using the Microsoft.Health.Fhir.R4 library to ensure compliance with the EHR’s expectations.

Got the backend choice: ASP.NET Core on .NET 8, with FHIR R4 endpoints built on Microsoft.Health.Fhir.R4. I'll record that.

When does version one need to be live? A fixed date helps us decide what must be in the first release, since anything not needed to stop double entry can wait. If there's no fixed date, we'll assume none.

Version one must be live by October 15, 2024, to align with the hospital group’s Q4 digital health rollout and avoid duplication during the upcoming flu season peak. This deadline means we must prioritize core functionality—single-entry nurse notes, real-time sync to Epic, and 15-minute SharePoint sync—while deferring advanced features like audit trails and raw data export to v1.1.

Thanks, the October 15, 2024 deadline is clear, and it helps set what goes into version one. I'm recording it now. Next I'll ask about the core behavior: when a ward nurse enters a note once, where should it appear?

When a nurse enters a note once in the new system, it must appear immediately in the Epic EHR as a new Clinical Note (using the FHIR Observation and Composition resources) and be synced to the SharePoint handover spreadsheet within 15 minutes via a scheduled Azure Function. The note must be tagged with the nurse’s Azure AD identity and the timestamp in UTC to ensure auditability and compliance with HIPAA and GDPR.

That's a clear picture of what happens when a note is entered once. Before we go on, is there a budget range for this project? It matters because it decides whether we build or buy the parts that are not core. If you're not sure, we'll leave it undecided for now.

Yes, the budget is capped at $280,000 for the full project lifecycle, including development, testing, and deployment through v1.1. This is sufficient to build the core integration using the in-house team and Azure services, but not enough to license a third-party workflow or EHR integration platform. We’ll stick with custom-built components for the FHIR gateway, SharePoint sync, and audit logging, while leveraging Azure AD and Azure Functions to minimize cost and complexity.

Thanks, the $280,000 cap through v1.1, with custom-built components, is recorded.

Next, let's cover what the system must do for each role. For a charge nurse or ward manager, what is the first thing they do when they open the system during a handover?

The first thing a charge nurse or ward manager sees when they open the system is a real-time dashboard listing all active wards, with a visual indicator showing the number of pending or incomplete notes for each, updated every 5 minutes via SignalR. They can drill down into any ward to view a time-ordered list of the most recent notes, filtered by the shift’s active nurses and sorted by entry time, with the ability to filter by status—“entered,” “synced,” or “failed.

Thanks for describing the charge nurse dashboard. Before we design for scale, how many people will use the system at launch, roughly? It decides how much capacity we need. Default if unsure: under 100.

At launch, approximately 140 ward nurses across four adult medical and surgical units will use the system, with peak concurrent usage estimated at 45 users during morning shift handovers. The backend will be designed to handle up to 200 concurrent users and 1,200 note entries per hour, with Azure App Service autoscaling enabled and Azure SQL Database provisioned for 500 DTUs to ensure responsiveness under load.
Thanks, that answers the launch scale question: about 140 ward nurses, with peak concurrency near 45 during handovers.

Understood. The system will be designed for 140 active users at launch, with capacity to scale to 200 concurrent users and support 1,200 note entries per hour, using Azure App Service autoscaling and a 500 DTU Azure SQL Database.

Compliance affects data storage, hosting and security requirements, so it's worth settling early. This system handles patient health information, so what regulations apply? Default if unsure: personal data under GDPR.

This system handles protected health information (PHI) under HIPAA, so we must comply with the U.S. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, including the Security Rule and the Privacy Rule. Data must be encrypted at rest using Azure Storage Service Encryption with customer-managed keys, and in transit using TLS 1.3. All access to patient data must be logged and audited via Azure Monitor, with retention of logs for at least 6 years.

The participant has already answered the compliance question: HIPAA, with the Security and Privacy Rules, encryption at rest and in transit, and six-year audit log retention. I'll record that now rather than ask again.

Noting for the record that the answer mentions GDPR-style data handling only as an assumption; I'll keep HIPAA as the governing regime.

Next, let's move on to the nurse's workflow when they enter a note: what happens if the Epic write fails?

If the write to Epic fails, the system will log the error with full context—including the FHIR resource ID, timestamp, and error code—and retry the operation up to three times with exponential backoff over 15 minutes. If all retries fail, the note is marked as “sync failed” in the local database, and an alert is sent to the charge nurse dashboard and the IT operations team via Azure Monitor. The nurse will receive a non-blocking notification in the UI suggesting they re-enter the note or confirm it’s already in Epic.

Thanks for the failure handling: three retries with exponential backoff over 15 minutes, then a "sync failed" status with alerts to the charge nurse dashboard and IT operations.

One gap remains. The Philips IntelliVue X4 integration has no authentication method specified. Default: Azure AD. That means the monitor connection would use the same identity platform as the rest of the system. Should we keep Azure AD for this integration?

Yes, we’ll use Azure AD for the Philips IntelliVue X4 integration, but only via a dedicated service account with a managed identity in Azure, not direct user login. The IntelliVue X4 will authenticate using OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow with a registered app in Azure AD, scoped to read only specific observation streams (e.g., vitals, SpO2, ECG) via a custom FHIR endpoint on the Philips platform. This maintains consistent identity governance and audit trails across all system components.

Thanks, Azure AD with a managed-identity service account, using client credentials and read-only access to observation streams, is recorded for the Philips integration.

Now the users. Besides ward nurses, who else needs to use the system, and what is the first thing they do in it? Start with the administrator, since their first action is still missing.

The administrator’s first action upon logging in is to view the system health dashboard in the admin portal, which displays real-time metrics: status of the Epic and SharePoint syncs, number of failed FHIR transactions in the last hour, and active Azure AD sessions, all updated every 30 seconds. They can drill into logs via Azure Monitor, reset sync statuses, and manage user roles through a secure, audited interface using Azure AD Group Management APIs.

The administrator's first action is clear: they open the system health dashboard, which refreshes every 30 seconds and shows Epic and SharePoint sync status, failed FHIR transactions in the last hour, and active sessions. Is the admin dashboard the only thing an administrator needs to see first, or do they also need to deal with a specific task, such as a failed note, when they log in?

The admin dashboard is the first thing they see, but it also includes a “Critical Alerts” section at the top that highlights any failed syncs, unacknowledged errors, or system-level issues—such as a failed FHIR endpoint or expired Azure AD credentials—immediately upon login. If a high-priority alert exists, the admin must acknowledge it within 15 minutes to trigger a notification to the IT operations team via Azure Monitor. This ensures no critical failure goes unnoticed during shift change.

Thanks, the "Critical Alerts" section at the top of the admin dashboard, with a 15-minute acknowledgement window, is recorded.

Now the user stories. Starting with the ward nurse, what is the one thing they most want from this system?

The one thing a ward nurse most wants is to enter a note once and know it’s safely and instantly reflected in both the EHR and the handover spreadsheet, without having to retype or verify the data in two places—eliminating the risk of missing the shift handover deadline or introducing transcription errors.
That's the core of the product. Can you walk me through the last time a nurse entered a note in the current process? Tell me the steps, which screens or tools were used, and roughly how long it took.

The nurse starts at the bedside with the Philips IntelliVue X4 monitor, where they observe a patient’s vital signs—heart rate, SpO2, respiratory rate—and record them manually in the bedside system. Then they walk to a desktop terminal, log into Epic using Azure AD, navigate to the patient’s chart, and manually enter the same vitals into a structured note using the EHR’s template. Next, they open the shared SharePoint handover spreadsheet, copy the data into the appropriate cell, and save it. This entire process takes about 12 minutes per patient during a busy shift, with frequent context switching and a risk of mismatched entries due to manual copying.

Thanks for walking through the current process. That 12-minute re-entry cycle is exactly the problem we're solving.

Finding: the Epic EHR integration has no authentication method specified yet. Default: Azure AD OAuth 2.0, the same identity platform used for SSO and the Philips integration. That means the backend obtains tokens from the hospital's Azure AD to call the Epic FHIR R4 endpoints, with no separate credentials to manage. Do you want to keep Azure AD OAuth 2.0 for Epic?

Noted: Epic will use Azure AD OAuth 2.0 for the FHIR connection.

Next, the charge nurse. When they open the ward dashboard at the start of a shift, what do they need to see first, and what do they do next?

When a charge nurse opens the ward dashboard at shift start, the first thing they see is a real-time list of all patients on their ward, with a color-coded status indicator: green for “note entered and synced,” yellow for “note entered but not synced,” and red for “no note entered.” They then click on the red or yellow entries to review the note content, confirm accuracy, and assign it to the next nurse in the handover chain—this triggers a notification to the next nurse’s dashboard.

The charge nurse flow is clear: a live ward list with green, yellow and red status, then review, confirm and reassign a note to the next nurse. Two things are still unclear: when a charge nurse reassigns a note, does the next nurse have to accept it, or is it assigned immediately? And should the red "no note entered" status show only for patients who need a note by a set time?

The reassignment is immediate and does not require acceptance by the next nurse—this avoids workflow delays during busy handovers. However, the system logs the reassignment with timestamp and user ID for audit purposes. The red status only applies to patients who haven’t had a note entered by 07:30 AM, the official start time for the morning shift, to prioritize urgency and ensure timely documentation. Any patient without a note by that time is flagged in the dashboard with a high-priority alert.

Thanks, reassignment is immediate with an audit log, and the red status applies only after 07:30 AM for patients without a note.

Now I'd like to turn the workflows we've covered into a numbered list of functional requirements. Which one do you think is most important for version one, the nurse entering a note once, or seeing it in Epic right away?

The most important requirement for version one is that the nurse enters a note once and it appears in Epic within 90 seconds—this is the core value proposition and the primary reason for building the system. If the note doesn’t appear in Epic promptly, the entire workflow collapses, regardless of whether the SharePoint sync happens on time. We’ll treat the Epic write as the success criterion for the note entry event, and the SharePoint sync as a secondary, idempotent process that runs on a 15-minute schedule.

Got it: the Epic write within 90 seconds is the success criterion for a note entry, and SharePoint is a secondary sync on a 15-minute schedule. Before I record that as a requirement, one question: when a nurse enters a note, what exactly must they see on screen to know it succeeded, and what should they see if it did not?

When a nurse enters a note, they immediately see a green confirmation banner with the message “Note saved and syncing to Epic” and a timestamp. If the sync to Epic completes within 90 seconds, the banner updates to “Note successfully synced to EHR.” If it fails after three retries, the banner turns red with “Note entered locally but failed to sync to EHR—please check the dashboard for details,” and a link to the note’s status in the system. All feedback is displayed in the same UI modal to avoid context switching.

Thanks for the feedback design. Recording the on-screen banner states now.

One gap remains in the red-status rule. It says a patient without a note by 07:30 AM is flagged, but it does not say what happens to a note entered after 07:30. Default: none, meaning the patient's status turns green as soon as the note is saved and the flag clears. That means a late note resolves the high-priority alert without any record that it was late. Should late notes clear the flag, or should the late entry stay recorded against the 07:30 deadline?

Noted: a note entered after 07:30 AM stays recorded against the 07:30 deadline, so the late entry is visible even after the red flag clears.

Next, the nurse's save flow. When a nurse saves a note and the Epic write takes longer than 90 seconds, does the nurse still get a saved confirmation right away, or do they have to wait on the screen?

The nurse gets an immediate “Note saved locally” confirmation in the UI, even if the Epic sync is still pending. This ensures the nurse knows their input is captured and can proceed with their workflow without waiting. The system then continues to retry the Epic write in the background, and the status is updated on-screen only when the sync completes or fails—no user action is required to continue.

Thanks, so the nurse gets an immediate "Note saved locally" confirmation and can keep working while the Epic write retries in the background. Before I record it, one question: if the background retries are still running when the nurse closes the modal or logs out, should the note still reach Epic?

Yes, the note must still reach Epic even if the nurse closes the modal or logs out—the system will retain the unsynced note in a retry queue in Azure SQL Database with a persistent job ID. The Azure Function responsible for the FHIR write will continue retrying the sync for up to 15 minutes after the initial save, and only mark it as failed if all retries are exhausted. This ensures no data is lost due to session timeouts or unexpected logouts.

Got it: a note keeps retrying in the background for up to 15 minutes, even after the nurse closes the modal or logs out, and is marked failed only when retries run out.

Next, the business rules. When a nurse saves a note for a patient who already has one for this shift, should the system add a second note or replace the first?

The system will replace the previous note for the same patient and shift, but only if the new note is submitted within 15 minutes of the first. This avoids redundant documentation while allowing correction of errors or updates based on newer vitals—critical for accuracy during fast-moving shifts. All prior notes are archived with a “replaced” status and timestamp, and the audit log will show the transition.

Thanks. So a second note replaces the first only within 15 minutes of it, and older notes are archived as "replaced" with a timestamp. What happens to a second note entered after the 15 minutes have passed: is it added as a separate note, or does the system block the entry until the nurse talks to the charge nurse?

A second note entered after 15 minutes is treated as a new, distinct observation and added as a separate entry in both Epic and SharePoint, with a clear timestamp and note type indicating it’s a follow-up. The system does not block the entry—there’s no need to escalate to a charge nurse unless the note content triggers a clinical alert. This preserves clinical continuity while supporting longitudinal tracking of changes in patient status.

Thanks, a note entered after 15 minutes is added as a separate follow-up entry with its own timestamp. Let's test that rule with an example. A nurse enters a note for bed 4 at 07:10, and a second note at 07:40 reports a new drop in blood pressure. Should both notes remain visible in Epic and SharePoint, with the 07:40 one marked as a follow-up?

Confirmed: both notes stay visible, and the 07:40 note is marked as a follow-up.

One edge case is still open. If the sync to Epic fails while a note is replacing an earlier one, which version should the charge nurse dashboard show, and should the replaced note stay in Epic? Default: the failed new note shows as failed, the earlier note stays active in Epic until the replacement succeeds, and the replaced note is archived only after that. Do you accept that default?

Yes, I accept the default: if the replacement fails, the original note remains active in Epic, the new note is marked as "failed to sync" in the local system, and the replaced version is archived with a status of "replaced pending sync" and a timestamp. The charge nurse dashboard will show the original note as current until the replacement is successfully synced, ensuring no data loss or confusion during shift change.

Thanks, that closes the replacement edge case: if the replacement fails, the original note stays active in Epic and the dashboard shows it as current.

Now let's move to acceptance criteria. For the core requirement, a nurse enters a note once and it appears in Epic: how would a tester confirm this is working? For example, by entering a note on a test patient and checking the Epic chart within 90 seconds?

Thanks. A plain "yes" leaves the test steps open, so I'll confirm the check as stated: a tester enters a note for a test patient, and the note appears in that patient's Epic chart within 90 seconds, with the nurse's Azure AD identity and a UTC timestamp. Does the tester also need to confirm that the nurse sees the green "Note saved and syncing to Epic" banner at entry?

Yes, the tester must also confirm that the nurse sees the green "Note saved and syncing to Epic" banner immediately upon saving, and that the banner updates to "Note successfully synced to EHR" within 90 seconds when the FHIR write completes—this validates both the local confirmation and the end-to-end sync. The test suite will include both UI and backend checks: the front-end message is verified via automated UI testing (Playwright), and the FHIR resource is validated in Epic’s audit log via a scripted query.

Thanks, the banner check and the 90-second update are clear. Let's go one level deeper on the failure path. A tester blocks the Epic connection for a test patient and saves a note: should the red banner "Note entered locally but failed to sync to EHR" appear only after the third retry, which takes up to 15 minutes, or sooner?

Confirmed: on a failed sync, the red banner appears only after the third retry, up to 15 minutes after the save.

A nurse who saves a note during an outage will see "Note saved locally" for up to 15 minutes before the failure appears. For a tester, the check is: block the Epic connection, save a note, and confirm that the red banner is absent for the first 15 minutes and appears only after the third retry fails.

Does a nurse also need to see a retry count or countdown during those 15 minutes, or is the "Note saved locally" message enough?

The "Note saved locally" message is sufficient—the system does not show a retry count or countdown to the nurse, as it could cause unnecessary anxiety or confusion during a high-pressure shift. Instead, the retry logic runs silently in the background, and the user only receives feedback when the outcome is final: either a green success banner or a red failure banner after three retries. This keeps the interface simple and focused on workflow continuity.

Thanks, so no retry count or countdown is shown, and the nurse sees only the "Note saved locally" message until the outcome is final.

Now the technical side. Your team is strong in C# and .NET 8, so the backend is set. For the front end, which is the first decision: should the nurse's web app be built with ASP.NET Core Razor Pages and server-rendered HTML, or as a single-page app in a JavaScript framework such as React? Default: Razor Pages, since it keeps everything in your team's C# skills.

I’ll choose React for the front end, even though it’s outside the team’s initial comfort zone, because the workflow requires real-time updates (e.g., sync status banners, dashboard refreshes), complex user interactions (note editing, reassignments), and a responsive design across mobile and desktop. We’ll use React with TypeScript, hosted in an Azure App Service with static file delivery, and we’ll pair the team with a senior front-end engineer for two weeks to ramp up on the stack. This ensures a better user experience and long-term maintainability, justifying the short-term learning curve.

Thanks, React with TypeScript on Azure App Service is recorded. Your reasons are sound, and the two-week pairing with a senior front-end engineer covers the learning curve. One point to check: your team's skills list has no front-end experience, so the pairing plan matters for the October 15 deadline.

Next, the database. The retry queue and note history both need to live in Azure SQL Database, so I'd like to know whether notes should be stored as one row per note with a status column, or as separate tables for notes, sync attempts and archived versions. Default: separate tables, so each retry and each replacement is traceable.

I confirm: separate tables are required. We’ll have a `Notes` table for active entries, a `SyncAttempts` table to log each FHIR write attempt with timestamp, status, and error code, and an `ArchivedNotes` table for replaced or failed notes with a `ReplacedBy` reference and `Status` (e.g., "replaced", "failed"). This structure enables full auditability, supports the 15-minute retry logic, and allows the charge nurse dashboard to show historical context without data loss. All tables will be in the same Azure SQL Database instance, with indexes on `PatientId`, `ShiftStart`, and `Status` for performance.

Confirmed: separate tables for notes, sync attempts and archived notes, all in one Azure SQL Database instance, indexed on PatientId, ShiftStart and Status.

Next, the sync trigger. When a nurse saves a note, should the Epic write start immediately from the web app, or should every note go through the persistent retry queue first, so the write and any retries run from the same place? Default: every note goes through the queue, which keeps retries alive after logout.

Before we wrap up, I still need an answer on the sync trigger: should every note go through the persistent retry queue first, or should the Epic write start directly from the web app? Once that's settled, I'll ask the closing question.

Every note must go through the persistent retry queue first—this ensures that even if the nurse logs out or closes the browser, the sync attempt remains in the system and continues to retry for up to 15 minutes. The web app immediately inserts the note into the `Notes` table and triggers a message to an Azure Service Bus queue, which is consumed by a dedicated Azure Function responsible for processing the FHIR write and enforcing the retry policy. This design decouples the UI from the retry logic and maintains reliability, consistency, and auditability across all failure scenarios.

Thanks. Here is what I captured. Nurses enter each ward note once, and it reaches Epic within 90 seconds and the SharePoint handover sheet within 15 minutes. Saves go through a persistent queue, with retries for up to 15 minutes, and failure appears only after the third retry. Follow-up notes after 15 minutes are added as separate entries. Charge nurses reassign notes immediately, and administrators get a health dashboard with critical alerts. The stack is React with TypeScript on Azure App Service and Azure SQL Database with separate Notes, SyncAttempts and ArchivedNotes tables. Some items still need follow-up, including front-end skills and the admin surface list. Please tell me anything I've got wrong or missed.

summary:
The system will run in a cloud account. The main pain point is the double entry of nurse notes, which takes 12 minutes per shift and causes a 7% error rate. The system must integrate with the Philips IntelliVue X4 bedside monitoring system (using Azure AD with a managed-identity service account, OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow, and read-only access to observation streams), the Epic EHR (FHIR R4 APIs, Azure AD OAuth 2.0), and a SharePoint handover spreadsheet with a 15-minute sync. Primary users are 140 ward nurses across four adult medical and surgical units, accessing the system via a web app with Azure AD single sign-on and role-based access control. Charge nurses and ward managers will have read-only access to notes on their assigned wards, while administrators will have full access to audit logs and system settings for troubleshooting and compliance.

The in-house team is proficient in C#, .NET 8, Azure Functions, Azure SQL Database, FHIR integration with Epic, Azure AD OAuth, Application Gateway and Azure Monitor. The backend will use ASP.NET Core on .NET 8, with FHIR R4 endpoints built on Microsoft.Health.Fhir.R4. Version one must be live by October 15, 2024, to align with the hospital group’s Q4 digital health rollout and avoid duplication during the upcoming flu season peak. This deadline means we must prioritize core functionality—single-entry nurse notes, real-time sync to Epic, and 15-minute SharePoint sync—while deferring advanced features like audit trails and raw data export to v1.1.

When a nurse enters a note once in the new system, it must appear immediately in the Epic EHR as a new Clinical Note (using the FHIR Observation and Composition resources) and be synced to the SharePoint handover spreadsheet within 15 minutes via a scheduled Azure Function. The note must be tagged with the nurse’s Azure AD identity and the timestamp in UTC to ensure auditability and compliance with HIPAA (including the Security and Privacy Rules, encryption at rest and in transit, and six-year audit log retention) and GDPR. The budget is capped at $280,000 for the full project lifecycle, including development, testing, and deployment through v1.1. This is sufficient to build the core integration using the in-house team and Azure services, but not enough to license a third-party workflow or EHR integration platform. We’ll stick with custom-built components for the FHIR gateway, SharePoint sync, and audit logging, while leveraging Azure AD and Azure Functions to minimize cost and complexity.

At launch, the system will handle up to 200 concurrent users and 1,200 note entries per hour, with Azure App Service autoscaling enabled and Azure SQL Database provisioned for 500 DTUs. If the write to Epic fails, the system will log the error and retry the operation up to three times with exponential backoff over 15 minutes. If all retries fail, the note is marked as “sync failed” in the local database, and an alert is sent to the charge nurse dashboard and the IT operations team via Azure Monitor. The nurse will receive a non-blocking notification in the UI suggesting they re-enter the note or confirm it’s already in Epic.

The first thing a charge nurse or ward manager sees when they open the system is a real-time dashboard listing all active wards, with a visual indicator showing the number of pending or incomplete notes for each, updated every 5 minutes via SignalR. They can drill down into any ward to view a time-ordered list of the most recent notes, filtered by the shift’s active nurses and sorted by entry time, with the ability to filter by status—“entered,” “synced,” or “failed.” The administrator’s first action upon logging in is to view the system health dashboard in the admin portal, which displays real-time metrics: status of the Epic and SharePoint syncs, number of failed FHIR transactions in the last hour, and active Azure AD sessions, all updated every 30 seconds. They can drill into logs via Azure Monitor, reset sync statuses, and manage user roles through a secure, audited interface using Azure AD Group Management APIs. The admin dashboard also includes a “Critical Alerts” section at the top that highlights any failed syncs, unacknowledged errors, or system-level issues—such as a failed FHIR endpoint or expired Azure AD credentials—immediately upon login. If a high-priority alert exists, the admin must acknowledge it within 15 minutes to trigger a notification to the IT operations team via Azure Monitor. This ensures no critical failure goes unnoticed during shift change.

The one thing a ward nurse most wants is to enter a note once and know it’s safely and instantly reflected in both the EHR and the handover spreadsheet, without having to retype or verify the data in two places—eliminating the risk of missing the shift handover deadline or introducing transcription errors. The current process involves the nurse starting at the bedside with the Philips IntelliVue X4 monitor, observing a patient’s vital signs, and recording them manually in the bedside system. Then they walk to a desktop terminal, log into Epic using Azure AD, navigate to the patient’s chart, and manually enter the same vitals into a structured note using the EHR’s template. Next, they open the shared SharePoint handover spreadsheet, copy the data into the appropriate cell, and save it. This entire process takes about 12 minutes per patient during a busy shift, with frequent context switching and a risk of mismatched entries due to manual copying.

When a charge nurse opens the ward dashboard at shift start, the first thing they see is a real-time list of all patients on their ward, with a color-coded status indicator: green for “note entered and synced,” yellow for “note entered but not synced,” and red for “no note entered.” They then click on the red or yellow entries to review the note content, confirm accuracy, and assign it to the next nurse in the handover chain—this triggers a notification to the next nurse’s dashboard. The reassignment is immediate and does not require acceptance by the next nurse—this avoids workflow delays during busy handovers. However, the system logs the reassignment with timestamp and user ID for audit purposes. The red status only applies to patients who haven’t had a note entered by 07:30 AM, the official start time for the morning shift, to prioritize urgency and ensure timely documentation. Any patient without a note by that time is flagged in the dashboard with a high-priority alert.

# Ward notes

Language: en · Path: technical · Generated: 2026-10-14T07:09:51.427Z

## Context

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| hosting | cloud |
| problem_metrics | 12 minutes per shift re-entry; 7% transcription error rate from a recent audit; documentation delays reported |
| existing_systems | Philips IntelliVue X4 bedside monitoring; Epic EHR 2023.01 via FHIR R4; SharePoint handover spreadsheet under Azure AD with read/write and a 15-minute scheduled sync |
| builder | team |
| team_skills | C#, .NET 8, Azure Functions, Azure SQL Database, FHIR integration with Epic, Azure AD OAuth 2.0, Azure Application Gateway, Azure Monitor |
| timeline | Version one must be live by October 15, 2024; defer audit trails and raw data export to v1.1. |
| budget | Capped at $280,000 for the full lifecycle through v1.1; custom-built components, no third-party workflow or EHR integration platform. |
| users_at_launch | About 140 ward nurses across four adult medical and surgical units; peak concurrency about 45 during morning handovers; designed for up to 200 concurrent users and 1,200 note entries per hour |
| compliance | HIPAA (Security Rule and Privacy Rule); encryption at rest with Azure Storage Service Encryption using customer-managed keys; TLS 1.3 in transit; all patient data access logged and audited via Azure Monitor with at least 6-year retention. |

## Product overview and problem

### Product overview and problem

Nurses currently enter clinical observations twice, once in the bedside monitoring system and again into the EHR and a SharePoint spreadsheet. This double entry takes about 12 minutes per patient each shift and results in a 7% transcription error rate, causing delays and inaccuracies in documentation. The product aims to let nurses enter each note just once and have it appear automatically in both Epic EHR and the handover spreadsheet, reducing time spent and improving data quality.

## Target users and roles

### Target users and roles

- **Ward nurse**: Enters clinical observations once per patient for their assigned ward, needing to avoid duplicate data entry.
- **Charge nurse**: Views all notes for assigned wards in read-only mode to monitor completeness and delays; can reassign notes to the next nurse.
- **Ward manager**: Views notes read-only for quality and timeliness oversight across wards.
- **Administrator**: Manages system health, user roles via Azure AD, resets sync statuses, and audits logs for compliance and troubleshooting.

## User stories

### User stories

- **US-1**: As a ward nurse, I want to enter a note once and see it in both Epic and the SharePoint handover spreadsheet without retyping.
- **US-2**: As a ward nurse, I want immediate confirmation that my note is saved and synced so I am confident it reached both systems.
- **US-3**: As a charge nurse, I want to view a live dashboard showing note status per patient and reassign notes immediately during handovers.
- **Sync-failure**: If an Epic write fails, it is retried 3 times over 15 minutes, with alerts sent to charge nurse and IT, and the nurse receives a non-blocking prompt to re-enter or confirm the note.
- **Current process**: Nurses read vitals from Philips IntelliVue X4, then manually enter data into Epic and the SharePoint spreadsheet, taking 12 minutes per patient.

## Functional requirements

### Functional requirements

This section lists the functional capabilities required to deliver the MVP. It covers note entry, synchronization, dashboards for nurses and managers, administration, and user feedback on sync status.

### MVP

- **FR-1** Nurse can enter a ward note once
  - Acceptance: A nurse submits one ward note and the system accepts it without a second entry screen
  - Acceptance: The note is attributed to the nurse's Azure AD identity with a UTC timestamp
  - Reason: Core value proposition
- **FR-2** Note appears in Epic EHR immediately
  - Acceptance: After a nurse submits a note, the note appears in the patient's Epic chart within 90 seconds
  - Reason: Epic write is the success criterion
- **FR-3** Note syncs to SharePoint handover spreadsheet within 15 minutes
  - Acceptance: A note reaches the SharePoint handover spreadsheet within 15 minutes of entry
  - Acceptance: Repeated sync runs do not create duplicate rows
  - Reason: Secondary sync
- **FR-4** Charge nurse or ward manager views a live ward dashboard
  - Acceptance: Dashboard lists all active wards with a pending/incomplete note count per ward
  - Acceptance: Counts refresh every 5 minutes via SignalR
  - Acceptance: Drill-down shows notes ordered by entry time, filterable by entered, synced or failed
- **FR-5** Charge nurse or ward manager views notes filtered by shift nurse and status
  - Acceptance: Notes list is filtered to the shift's active nurses
  - Acceptance: Notes are sorted by entry time
  - Acceptance: Status filter offers entered, synced and failed
- **FR-6** Administrator views a live system health dashboard
  - Acceptance: Administrator opens the system health dashboard
  - Acceptance: Dashboard shows status of Epic and SharePoint syncs
  - Acceptance: Dashboard shows number of failed FHIR transactions in last hour
  - Acceptance: Dashboard shows active Azure AD sessions
  - Acceptance: Dashboard refreshes every 30 seconds
- **FR-7** Nurse enters a ward note once and it reaches both systems
  - Acceptance: Nurse enters a note in the bedside system
  - Acceptance: Note appears in Epic EHR immediately
  - Acceptance: Note syncs to SharePoint handover spreadsheet within 15 minutes
  - Acceptance: Nurse does not re-enter the same data in two places
- **FR-8** Charge nurse reassigns a note to the next nurse
  - Acceptance: Charge nurse reassigns a note and the next nurse's dashboard shows it immediately
  - Acceptance: Reassignment is recorded with timestamp and user ID
- **FR-9** Nurse sees save and sync feedback in one modal
  - Acceptance: After a note is saved, a green banner shows 'Note saved and syncing to Epic' with a timestamp
  - Acceptance: When the Epic sync completes within 90 seconds, the banner shows 'Note successfully synced to EHR'
  - Acceptance: When the sync fails after three retries, the banner turns red with 'Note entered locally but failed to sync to EHR' and a link to the note's status
- **FR-10** Nurse saves a note before Epic confirms it
  - Acceptance: When the Epic write has not completed, the nurse sees 'Note saved locally' at once and can continue without waiting
  - Acceptance: The Epic write keeps retrying in the background with no user action required

- **FR-11** Nurse enters a note and it appears in Epic within 90 seconds

  - Acceptance: The Epic entry carries the nurse's Azure AD identity and a UTC timestamp

- **FR-12** Nurse sees a sync failure only after the third retry fails
  - Acceptance: Block the Epic connection, save a note, and confirm the red banner is absent for the first 15 minutes
  - Acceptance: Confirm the red banner appears only after the third retry fails
  - Reason: Defines when a sync failure becomes visible to the nurse.

## Business rules

### Business rules

- Red "no note entered" status only applies to patients without a note by 07:30 AM; these are flagged as high priority.
- Notes entered after 07:30 AM remain recorded against the 07:30 deadline to preserve timely documentation.
- Unsynced notes remain in a persistent retry queue and retry syncing for up to 15 minutes post save, even if the nurse logs out.
- A duplicate note submitted within 15 minutes replaces the earlier note, which is archived with a replaced status and timestamp.
- Follow-up notes submitted after 15 minutes are entered as separate notes with their own timestamps and types; both are visible.
- If a replacement note fails sync, the original note remains active in Epic; the replacement is marked failed locally and archived pending sync.
- Nurses see only simple retry feedback: a green banner on save and success, or a red banner after failure; retry counts are hidden.

## Technical requirements

### Technical requirements

The system will be hosted in a cloud account using Azure services. The in-house team will build using C#, .NET 8, ASP.NET Core backend, Azure Functions for sync processing, Azure SQL Database with separate tables for notes, sync attempts, and archives, and React with TypeScript frontend hosted on Azure App Service. Authentication uses hospital Azure AD single sign-on and OAuth 2.0. Note sync to Epic uses FHIR R4 APIs with Azure AD authentication. The frontend team pairs with a senior front-end engineer for two weeks to ramp up. Sync retries are managed via an Azure Service Bus queue and Azure Functions for reliable background processing.

## Data requirements

### Data requirements

- **Notes**: Fields include PatientId, ShiftStart, Status, and ReplacedBy; linked to SyncAttempts and ArchivedNotes.
- **SyncAttempts**: Include timestamp, status, error code; linked to Notes.
- **ArchivedNotes**: Include ReplacedBy, Status; linked to Notes.
- Data stored in Azure SQL Database, indexed on PatientId, ShiftStart, and Status for performance.

## Integrations

### Integrations

- **Philips IntelliVue X4**: Bedside monitor providing clinical observations via read-only streams with Azure AD OAuth 2.0 client credentials using a dedicated managed-identity service account.
- **Epic EHR 2023.01**: Clinical record system accessed via FHIR R4 APIs authenticated with Azure AD OAuth 2.0.
- **SharePoint handover spreadsheet**: Read/write access via Azure AD with scheduled 15-minute sync.

## Security and privacy

### Security and privacy

- Web app uses hospital Azure AD single sign-on.
- Role-based access control limits note entry to nurses assigned to wards; read-only roles for charge nurses and managers.
- HIPAA compliance includes Security and Privacy Rules.
- Data encrypted at rest using Azure Storage Service Encryption with customer-managed keys.
- Data in transit secured with TLS 1.3.
- Audit logs of all patient data access retained for six years via Azure Monitor.

## Non-functional requirements

### Non-functional requirements

- Budget capped at $280,000 to cover development, testing, and deployment through version 1.1.
- System designed to support 140 users at launch, peak concurrency 45, scaling up to 200 concurrent users and 1,200 note entries per hour.
- The system shall meet the October 15, 2024 live deployment deadline.

## Administrative surface

### Administrative surface

- System health dashboard with real-time metrics: Epic and SharePoint sync status, failed FHIR transactions in the last hour, active Azure AD sessions.
- Dashboard refreshes every 30 seconds.
- Critical Alerts section atop the dashboard requires acknowledgement within 15 minutes, which triggers IT operations notification.
- Admins can drill into Azure Monitor logs, reset sync statuses, and manage user roles securely and with audit logging via Azure AD Group Management APIs.

## MVP scope

### MVP scope

The MVP version includes the ability for nurses to enter notes once with real-time sync to Epic and a 15-minute sync to the SharePoint handover spreadsheet, real-time dashboards for charge nurses and ward managers, system administration dashboard with critical alerting, and adherence to HIPAA compliance. Version one must be live by October 15, 2024.

## Implementation phases

### Implementation phases

The implementation is planned in phases to deliver a functioning MVP by October 15, 2024. Early phases focus on core note entry, syncing to Epic and SharePoint, and nurse dashboard. Later phases build administrative dashboards, alerts, and full retry mechanisms.

### Phase 1: Core note entry and synchronization

## Open questions

### Open questions
